title: Stream liveness heartbeats, graceful drain, and OS-signal integration for Go SDK
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary:
Implement a robust liveness and graceful-drain surface in the Go SDK streaming client to avoid leaked goroutines and opaque hangs in customer apps. This ticket covers: heartbeat/keepalive pinging, explicit Drain semantics that finish inflight processing before closing, integration with OS signals (SIGTERM/SIGINT) to map signals to context cancellation for graceful shutdown, and clearer timeout/cancellation ergonomics for long-lived streams.

Motivation and user stories:
- Customers running the Go SDK in containerized services report lingering goroutines and unclean shutdowns when processes receive SIGTERM during deployment rollouts.
- Long-lived streams (chat/assist) should be stoppable with a deterministic drain so server processing and metrics are consistent.
- Developers need simple, composable primitives: context-aware Close/Drain and sensible defaults for heartbeat intervals and connection deadlines.

Design goals and constraints:
- Minimal API surface changes; prefer additive methods on existing Stream object.
- Works with both HTTP chunked streaming and gRPC transports used by Redwood.
- Defaults that are safe for typical services (heartbeat 30s, missed-heartbeat threshold 3) but fully configurable per-client and per-stream.
- Avoid false-positive disconnects on mobile/poor networks: expose conservative default backoffs and jitter.
- Provide observability hooks (metrics and trace events) to make failures debuggable.

API changes (proposed):
- Add to existing streaming client type (StreamClient or Stream):
  - Drain(ctx context.Context) error  // waits for inflight messages to complete, respecting ctx
  - CloseWithContext(ctx context.Context) error // initiates immediate close, but allows a deadline via ctx
  - SetHeartbeat(interval time.Duration, threshold int) // optional tuning
  - OnHeartbeat(func()) // callback for testing/observability

Goroutine and cancellation model:
- Current model: separate read and write goroutines with a shared done channel. We will:
  - Introduce a parent context (streamCtx) created per-Stream that is canceled on any terminal condition (fatal network error, explicit CloseWithContext, or mapped OS signal).
  - Drain will: stop accepting new user writes, wait for in-flight writes and read processing loops to finish, and then close transport. The Drain call will be context-aware and return context.DeadlineExceeded if it times out.
  - CloseWithContext will short-circuit Drain and force transport close after ctx expires.

Heartbeat/keepalive protocol:
- Transport-agnostic heartbeat: for HTTP chunked we send an empty chunk or ping frame if supported; for gRPC we use the underlying stream KeepAlive or an application-level ping message.
- Default interval: 30s, default missed threshold: 3 (=> ~90s before considered dead).
- Heartbeat implementation lives in a dedicated goroutine that writes non-blocking pings; a missed-write counter triggers a streamCtx cancel after threshold.
- Jitter: add ±20% jitter to interval to reduce synchronized failover storms.

OS signal integration and lifecycle hooks:
- Provide a helper in the SDK: HandleSignalsForStream(ctx, stream) that does:
  - Listens for SIGTERM, SIGINT and maps them to canceling a context returned to the user.
  - When signal seen, call stream.Drain(signalCtx) with a conservative timeout (default 20s) so other frameworks can finish in-flight work.
- Documentation will recommend service authors explicitly wire their main shutdown path to a cancelable context using the SDK helper.

Timeout semantics and Read/Write deadlines:
- Where the transport supports deadlines (net.Conn), the SDK will set ReadDeadline/WriteDeadline before blocking network calls, extrapolated from heartbeat interval and an internal per-call timeout (configurable).
- For streaming operations that may legitimately be idle for long periods (e.g., user typing multi-minute gaps), the heartbeat keeps the connection alive while allowing read calls to remain blocking.

Retry and resume considerations:
- Short network blips should not immediately drop the stream. On transient failure we will attempt up to N reconnects (configurable, default 3) with exponential backoff and then surface an error.
- Resume tokens: not in scope for this ticket, but design will emit a metric and trace ID to allow higher-level resume implementations to pick up where left off.

Observability and metrics:
- Emit metrics per-stream: heartbeat_sent, heartbeat_missed, drain_duration_seconds, shutdown_signal_received, stream_reconnect_attempts, stream_final_status.
- Add tracing spans for Drain and CloseWithContext so rollouts can be correlated with infra events.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for: heartbeat scheduling, missed-heartbeat detection, Drain happy-path and timeout path, CloseWithContext forced close.
- Integration test: run a small HTTP chunked server that simulates slow consumer and verify Drain completes and goroutines are cleaned up (use go test -race).
- Chaos test: inject dropped packets and ensure default retry/backoff keeps stream alive for short blips but fails after configured attempts.

Benchmarks and early results (notes from PoC):
- PoC added heartbeat goroutine and Drain path. Bench micro-runs show p95 CPU for a long-lived stream increased by ~0.4% per stream (acceptable).
- On teardown, Drain reduced leaked goroutines from ~3 per stream to 0 in the test harness.

Docs and SDK examples:
- Add example showing: start stream -> wire HandleSignalsForStream in main -> gracefully drain on SIGTERM with 15s deadline -> report metrics.
- FAQ entry: choosing heartbeat interval and tradeoffs for mobile vs server deployments.

Rollout plan:
- Merge behind feature flag (env var: REDWOOD_GO_SDK_STREAM_DRAIN=enabled) and enable for 10% of users.
- Monitor drain_duration_seconds and stream_final_status errors for regressions for 72 hours.
- Ramp to 100% if no regressions.

Risks and open questions:
- Heartbeat false positives on cell-edge networks: mitigate by conservative defaults and clear docs.
- Interoperability with third-party reverse proxies that terminate idle connections earlier: document recommended proxy configs (TCP keepalive, proxy timeouts > missed-heartbeat threshold).
- API ergonomics: some users may prefer simpler Close() only; keep Close() as alias to CloseWithContext(context.Background()) to preserve backwards compatibility.

Follow-ups (subsequent tickets):
- Resume-token protocol and automatic stateful resume (large).
- Per-tenant heartbeat tuning based on observed RTTs.

Artifacts and links:
- PoC PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/go-sdk/pull/1298
- Design doc (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SDK/Go+stream+liveness+design

Acceptance criteria:
- New Drain and CloseWithContext APIs implemented and documented.
- Heartbeat default enabled but tunable, with metrics emitted.
- Signal helper provided and example in README.
- Unit + integration tests validating goroutine cleanup and Drain semantics.

2026-03-07 - Design review by Jordan Kim: suggested using jitter for heartbeat interval and exposing metrics; added to design.
2026-03-10 - Integration test failure: reverse proxy in test harness closed idle connection before missed-heartbeat threshold; adjusted test and documented proxy recommendations.
